claims.text: The eutectic high-entropy alloy contains distinct interspersed phases with different electrochemical nobility and passivation capacities.
Mechanical wear cyclically removes protective oxide or passivation layers.
Wear-induced film removal occurs particularly on the less noble phase.
Removal of the protective film exposes fresh reactive surfaces that corrode rapidly.
Potential differences between the constituent phases cause localized galvanic corrosion after wear-induced depassivation.
Localized corrosion preferentially damages phase boundaries or interphase structural interfaces.
Corrosion-induced interfacial damage and microstructural softening amplify subsequent wear.
Repeated wear prevents a stable protective film from reforming, producing a self-reinforcing wear-corrosion cycle.
Elevated temperature affects the stability and reformation of the protective oxide layers.
The proposed mechanism requires wear severe enough to continuously remove the oxide or passive layers.
The proposed mechanism requires sufficient electrochemical contrast between phases to create significant galvanic coupling.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion will produce greater total mass loss than either isolated wear or isolated corrosion.
The wear component under coupled exposure will exceed the wear response measured in an inert or non-corrosive medium.
The corrosion current density under coupled exposure will exceed that measured during corrosion without mechanical wear.
The total degradation rate under simultaneous exposure will exceed the sum of the independently measured wear and corrosion contributions.
A comparison among isolated wear, isolated corrosion, and simultaneous wear-corrosion at matched temperature can test for a synergistic contribution.
